newsitem.title: JAPAN: Top Japan minister calls for slightly weaker yen.
newsitem.headline: Top Japan minister calls for slightly weaker yen.

text.p: A senior Japanese government minister in charge of reforming the government bureaucracy said on Tuesday the yen should be "slightly cheaper" than it is at present in order to help private industry.

Kabun Muto, director-general of the Management and Coordination Agency, told a group of foreign reporters at a briefing that a fall in the yen was needed to make Japanese companies less likely to move production overseas.
"I believe the yen should be slightly cheaper than it is today," he said.
He said that in the longer-term, it was important to maintain "a reasonable level for the yen." He did not offer a specific figure.
He also said he was worried about the role of the yen in the long-term. Between the dollar and the planned introduction of the euro "the Japanese currency may be forgotten," he said.
Muto's agency, which reports directly to the prime minister's office, is responsible for administrative reform as part of the government's plan to reduce spending and to deregulate the economy.
He said the government restructuring plan announced earlier on Tuesday was aimed at eliminating the price gap between Japan and overseas countries.
He said it was vital to reduce government spending or raise taxes to avoid new debt he estimated at 48 trillion yen for the 1996 fiscal year.
But he said that even a modest increase in the national sales tax from three percent to five percent planned for next April was extremely difficult to push through.
He noted that consumption tax levels were sharply higher in European countries.
"We just have to wonder why at this five percent level we have to be criticised all around, but this is the reality," he said.
"Government finances are in a very difficult state," he said.

He also said that the current goal of cutting 5.11 percent of central government jobs should be the minimum target. He said the group looking at administrative reform would issue an interim report on January 17, 1997.
He said that Japan must look to new sectors of "the information age" and not rely on "old industries."
